title: The Influence of Light Colour Temperatures on Interior Design Student Performance in Classroom Studies
central_proposition: Light colour temperatures significantly impact interior design students' perceived spatial quality, social adaptation, and individual productivity in classroom studio settings, with high colour temperatures generally leading to more positive outcomes.

concept_definitions.name: Light Colour Temperatures
concept_definitions.definition: The perceived warmth or coolness of light, categorized as low (warm white), daylight, and high (cool white/spaciousness), influencing physiological and psychological reactions.

concept_definitions.name: Spatial Quality
concept_definitions.definition: Students' perception of the overall spaciousness of the studio, the amount of natural light entering, and the brightness level.

concept_definitions.name: Social Adaptation
concept_definitions.definition: Students' perceived level of comfort, ease of collaboration with peers, and level of distraction by external factors in the classroom studio.

concept_definitions.name: Individual Productivity
concept_definitions.definition: Students' motivation to work, efficiency when completing tasks, and feeling fatigued or tired in the classroom studio.

argument_structure: The paper introduces the critical role of lighting in educational environments, reviews existing literature on how light colour temperatures affect human physiology, psychology, and performance, and then proposes a conceptual framework with three testable hypotheses. It subsequently describes an empirical survey methodology, presents statistical results, and discusses these findings in relation to the initial hypotheses and broader implications for design.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Different light colour temperatures are proposed to influence human physiological and psychological reactions. High colour temperatures (daylight/cool white) are hypothesized to mimic natural lighting, offering higher contrast and brightness, which leads to increased attentiveness, focus, and productivity, and reduced fatigue. Low colour temperatures (warm white) are hypothesized to create a comfortable and personal ambiance, fostering social cooperation and communication. These effects are mediated through impacts on physical and mental health, mood, and various cognitive processes.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Daylight used in the lighting of design studios positively affects the 'spatial quality' perception of students compared to high colour temperatures.
Low light colour temperatures used in the lighting of design studios positively affect the 'social adaptation' perception of students.
High-light colour temperatures used in the lighting of design studios increase the 'individual productivity' perception of students.
bridge_warrants: Lighting conditions significantly impact physical and mental health, and their dynamic alterations have a favourable impact on human well-being.
Different light colour temperatures influence individuals' physiological and psychological reactions.
High CCT is related to greater attentiveness and productivity, while warm white (low CCT) is related to relaxation.
Various light colour temperatures can impact cognitive, emotional, and visual processes.
Higher correlated colour temperatures (CCT) light contributes to substantial improvements in children's performance of task-switching.
Natural light fosters an increased feeling of satisfaction and health.
Warm lighting improves social behaviour and satisfaction among consumers.
High colour temperatures (5000K) lead to more effective cognitive tasks and greater attentiveness.
Higher correlated colour temperature (CCT) light sources improve cognitive performance in individuals with Alzheimer's disease.
model_structure: The proposed conceptual framework posits that light colour temperature (antecedent) directly influences students' spatial perception, social adaptation, and individual productivity (consequents) in design studios. It also suggests that individual characteristics (age, gender, prior lighting experience) and the nature of the task carried out in the design studio may moderate these relationships.
limitations: The sample size was limited to 124 interior design students from a specific university, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to a larger population.
The study relied on self-reported data, which could be subject to biases or inaccuracies.
The study focused only on the impact of light colour temperatures and did not consider other potential factors that could influence students' experiences in design studios.
